concept_html:
A fixture is a function decorated with @pytest.fixture. A test asks for it by naming it as a parameter, and pytest calls the fixture and passes in the result:

@pytest.fixture
def respondents() -> pd.DataFrame:
    return pd.DataFrame({"respondent_id": ["R1", "R2"], "final_weight": [1.0, 3.0]})


def test_total_weight(respondents: pd.DataFrame) -> None:
    assert respondents["final_weight"].sum() == 4.0

By default a fixture runs once per test, so every test gets a fresh object. A test can change it without touching any other test.

Use yield when something must be cleaned up. Code before yield is setup. Code after it is teardown, and pytest runs it even when the test fails.

scope="module" or scope="session" builds the object once and shares it. Use that only for things that are expensive and that no test changes, such as the SparkSession in lesson A9-L1. A shared object that one test changes makes results depend on the order tests run in.

Put fixtures that several files use in conftest.py. Tests in that folder and its subfolders can use them without an import.

pytest ships built-in fixtures. tmp_path gives each test a fresh temporary directory as a pathlib.Path. monkeypatch changes settings and undoes the change afterwards (lesson B19-L7).

When tests need many slightly different inputs, write a factory fixture. It returns a function that builds the data, with defaults for everything, so each test states only what matters to it:

@pytest.fixture
def make_respondents():
    def make(weights: list[float]) -> pd.DataFrame:
        ids = [f"R{i}" for i in range(1, len(weights) + 1)]
        return pd.DataFrame({"respondent_id": ids, "final_weight": weights})
    return make

solution_lines: import pandas as pd
import pytest
def in_scope_weight(df: pd.DataFrame) -> float:
"""Total final_weight of in-scope rows."""
return float(df.loc[df["in_scope"], "final_weight"].sum())
@pytest.fixture
def make_respondents():
"""Factory for small respondent frames with sensible defaults."""
def make(weights: list[float], in_scope: list[bool] | None = None) -> pd.DataFrame:
ids = [f"R{i}" for i in range(1, len(weights) + 1)]
flags = in_scope if in_scope is not None else [True] * len(weights)
return pd.DataFrame(
{
"respondent_id": ids,
"final_weight": [float(w) for w in weights],
"in_scope": flags,
}
)
return make
def test_in_scope_weight_skips_out_of_scope(make_respondents) -> None:
df = make_respondents([1.0, 3.0], in_scope=[True, False])
assert in_scope_weight(df) == 1.0

title: Fixtures, shared setup without shared state
why_html: A QA test suite shared one session-scoped DataFrame of 500 respondents across 40 tests. One test capped the weights in place to check the cap function. On a laptop the tests ran in file order and passed. In CI a plugin ran them in random order, and three weight-total tests failed about one run in four. The team spent two days calling the failures "flaky" before they found the in-place change. Function scope fixed it in one line.
